nodes.name: Ampere
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the elementary charge e to 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ coulombs, where the coulomb is ampere-seconds.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.3.
nodes.etymology: Named after André-Marie Ampère, French physicist and a founder of electromagnetism.

nodes.name: Candela
nodes.currentDefinition: The luminous intensity, in a given direction, of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540×10¹² Hz and has a radiant intensity in that direction of 1/683 watt per steradian.
nodes.currentSource: 16th CGPM (1979), Resolution 3; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.7.
nodes.etymology: From Latin 'candela', meaning candle.

nodes.name: Degree Celsius
nodes.currentDefinition: A unit of thermodynamic temperature equal in magnitude to the kelvin, with its zero point set at 273.15 K (the ice point of water) instead of absolute zero.
nodes.currentSource: 9th CGPM (1948); BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.
nodes.etymology: Named after Anders Celsius, who proposed a related centigrade scale in 1742 (originally with the scale inverted — 0 at boiling, 100 at freezing).
nodes.cursedness: Same-sized degree as the kelvin, different zero — see the kelvin-celsius relationship for why they were historically conflated. Celsius's own original 1742 scale ran backwards from today's.

nodes.name: Coulomb
nodes.currentDefinition: The quantity of electricity carried in one second by a current of one ampere.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb, for his law of electrostatic force.

nodes.name: Farad
nodes.currentDefinition: The capacitance of a capacitor between the plates of which there appears a difference of potential of one volt when it is charged by a quantity of electricity of one coulomb.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Michael Faraday, for his contributions to electromagnetism and electrochemistry.

nodes.name: Henry
nodes.currentDefinition: The inductance of a closed circuit in which an electromotive force of one volt is produced when the electric current in the circuit varies uniformly at a rate of one ampere per second.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Joseph Henry, who discovered electromagnetic self-inductance independently of Faraday.

nodes.name: Hertz
nodes.currentDefinition: The frequency of a periodic phenomenon of which the period is one second.
nodes.currentSource: 11th CGPM (1960), Resolution 12; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Heinrich Hertz, who first conclusively demonstrated the existence of electromagnetic waves.
nodes.cursedness: Dimensionally identical to the becquerel (also inverse seconds), but the two are never interchanged — see the kelvin-celsius relationship note for the pattern; a hertz-becquerel relationship entry covering this is queued in PROGRESS.md.

nodes.name: Joule
nodes.currentDefinition: The work done when the point of application of a force of one newton is displaced a distance of one metre in the direction of the force.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after James Prescott Joule, for his work on the mechanical equivalent of heat.

nodes.name: Katal
nodes.currentDefinition: The catalytic activity that increases the rate of conversion of a specified chemical reaction by one mole per second in a specified assay system.
nodes.currentSource: 21st CGPM (1999), Resolution 12; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: From 'catalysis', via Greek 'katalyein', meaning to dissolve/loosen.
nodes.cursedness: The newest of the SI derived units with special names, added in 1999 specifically to standardize enzyme-activity measurements in biochemistry — most SI derived units are two centuries older.

nodes.name: Kelvin
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Boltzmann constant k to 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K, where the joule is kg·m²·s⁻².
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4.
nodes.etymology: Named after William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin, who proposed an absolute temperature scale in 1848.

nodes.name: Kilogram
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Planck constant h to 6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s, which is kg·m²·s⁻¹.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.2.
nodes.etymology: From French 'kilogramme', from Greek 'khilioi' (thousand) + 'gramma' (small weight).
nodes.cursedness: The only SI base unit whose name contains a prefix ('kilo-'), a historical artifact of the gram being defined first and later found too small to be practical as the base unit.

nodes.name: Lumen
nodes.currentDefinition: The luminous flux emitted into a solid angle of one steradian by a point source with a uniform intensity of one candela.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: From Latin 'lumen', meaning light.

nodes.name: Lux
nodes.currentDefinition: The illuminance produced by a luminous flux of one lumen uniformly distributed over a surface of one square metre.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: From Latin 'lux', meaning light.

nodes.name: Metre
nodes.currentDefinition: Length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.
nodes.currentSource: 17th CGPM (1983), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.1.
nodes.etymology: From Greek 'metron', meaning measure.

nodes.name: Mole
nodes.currentDefinition: Defined by fixing the numerical value of the Avogadro constant N_A to 6.02214076×10²³ per mole.
nodes.currentSource: 26th CGPM (2018), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.5.
nodes.etymology: From German 'Molekül', coined by Wilhelm Ostwald around 1900 as a short form of 'gram-molecule'.
nodes.cursedness: Despite being clearly dimensionless (it's just Avogadro's number of something), the mole is counted as its own SI base unit rather than a bare number — a quirk chemistry insisted on.

nodes.name: Newton
nodes.currentDefinition: The force which gives a mass of one kilogram an acceleration of one metre per second squared.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Isaac Newton, in recognition of his work on classical mechanics.

nodes.name: Ohm
nodes.currentDefinition: The electric resistance between two points of a conductor when a constant potential difference of one volt, applied between these two points, produces a current of one ampere.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Georg Simon Ohm, for his law relating voltage, current, and resistance.

nodes.name: Pascal
nodes.currentDefinition: The pressure produced by a force of one newton applied uniformly over an area of one square metre.
nodes.currentSource: 14th CGPM (1971), Resolution 7; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Blaise Pascal, for his work on fluids and pressure.

nodes.name: Radian
nodes.currentDefinition: The plane angle between two radii of a circle which cut off on the circumference an arc equal in length to the radius — an arc-length-over-radius ratio, treated as dimensionless.
nodes.currentSource: 11th CGPM (1960), Resolution 12; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.3.
nodes.etymology: From Latin 'radius'.
nodes.cursedness: The radian is a metre-per-metre ratio, so SI treats it as dimensionless and usually drops it from equations entirely — but this is a choice, not a necessity. There's a competing, equally valid convention where the number 1 means one full revolution (used for rpm etc.), off from the radian convention by a factor of 2π. Angular momentum and torque only end up sharing units with energy because SI's convention quietly discards the radian.

nodes.name: Second
nodes.currentDefinition: Duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of the caesium-133 atom.
nodes.currentSource: 13th CGPM (1967/68), Resolution 1; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.1.
nodes.etymology: From Latin 'secunda pars minuta', 'second small part' (of an hour), following 'prima pars minuta', the minute.

nodes.name: Siemens
nodes.currentDefinition: The electrical conductance of a conductor in which a current of one ampere flows when a potential difference of one volt is applied — the reciprocal of the ohm.
nodes.currentSource: 14th CGPM (1971), Resolution 7; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Ernst Werner von Siemens, industrialist and founder of the Siemens company.

nodes.name: Steradian
nodes.currentDefinition: The solid angle which, having its vertex at the centre of a sphere, cuts off an area on the surface of the sphere equal to that of a square with sides of length equal to the radius of the sphere — an area-over-radius-squared ratio, treated as dimensionless.
nodes.currentSource: 11th CGPM (1960), Resolution 12; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.3.
nodes.etymology: From Greek 'stereos' (solid) + 'radian'.
nodes.cursedness: The 3D counterpart to the radian's cursedness: a genuinely dimensionless area-over-length-squared ratio that SI nonetheless gives its own named unit, feeding directly into the lumen (candela × steradian) as if it carried real dimension.

nodes.name: Tesla
nodes.currentDefinition: The magnetic flux density given by a magnetic flux of one weber per square metre.
nodes.currentSource: 11th CGPM (1960), Resolution 12; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Nikola Tesla, for his contributions to the design of the modern alternating-current electricity supply system.

nodes.name: Volt
nodes.currentDefinition: The difference of electric potential between two points of a conducting wire carrying a constant current of one ampere, when the power dissipated between these points is one watt.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Alessandro Volta, inventor of the first chemical battery.

nodes.name: Watt
nodes.currentDefinition: The power which gives rise to the production of energy at the rate of one joule per second.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after James Watt, for his improvements to the steam engine.
nodes.cursedness: kg·m²·s⁻³ is the joule's parent unit divided by time again — this exact chain (kg·m/s² → kg·m²/s² → kg·m²/s³) is the whole reason products like the kilowatt-hour feel so unintuitive: they multiply back by time instead of dividing, undoing part of this chain.

nodes.name: Weber
nodes.currentDefinition: The magnetic flux which, linking a circuit of one turn, produces in it an electromotive force of one volt as it is reduced to zero at a uniform rate in one second.
nodes.currentSource: CIPM (1946), Resolution 2; BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019).
nodes.etymology: Named after Wilhelm Eduard Weber, for his work on electromagnetism.

links.note:
The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size — a change of 1 K equals
a change of 1 °C — they only differ in where zero sits: 0 K is absolute
zero, while 0 °C is set at 273.15 K (the ice point of water). Historically,
temperature and heat were conflated for a long time, and Anders Celsius's
original 1742 proposal even ran the scale backwards from today's (0 at the
boiling point of water, 100 at freezing) before it was inverted shortly
after his death. The 2019 redefinition of the kelvin via the Boltzmann
constant left the Celsius scale's offset definition untouched, so Celsius
is now formally defined as an offset SI-derived unit built directly on the
kelvin rather than as its own independent base quantity.
links.sourceRef: BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (2019), sec. 2.3.4 and Annex.
